title: Losing the Pima language and the return to Arizona
summary: Visiting his brother, Moore found they could not remember Pima; his uncle sent him home, where he broke down at the table, then listened to records in Tucson music stores.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Yea, I think that's, that was, that was them. And, between that and then -- I would still go back to Blue Island to visit my brother, and we talked about the old days in, in a -- on the reservation. How our, our language began. We can't remember our language because we didn't have no occassion to talk anymore Pima. And I told him that I could sing our chants like Old Skomuck during when we were, we were kids on the reservation.

I see. That was quite a traumatic time for you then, dealing with the fact that you wern't remembering the language because you weren't using it, and also traveling around Chicago and seeing some of the names of the musicians and
the famous band leaders on the marquees. You never got a chance to hear them, I guess, at that time.

No, no I didn't because, as I said, I, I go back, I went back to the re -- not the reser -- to Blue Island to, to visit my, my brother, and that one time my uncle ran into me, and he said to me it was gettin' on to school time in September. So he asked me what I wanted to go to school, or you want to go home. So I said I want to go home. So my uncle said, "All right, I'll buy you a ticket." And his advice to me was "go back to school when you get home." So that's how I came back to Arizona. And talk about trauma! At that time when I got into Arizona, I was let out at Tucson. My mother had remarried, and I want to -- when we had a meal at the table, I asked, I asked the name of the salt in Pima -- the name of this in Pima, the name of this in Pima. And, talk about trauma, I just broke down and said I'm sorry I can't remember my language, you know. And they begin to know that -- realize that I been through a trauma about living the two types of lives like in Chicago and back to Arizona with the Indians. And, at that time, I used to go to the stores in Tucson and listen to records in the music stores. And I used to hear Guy Lombardo and Meyer Davis and quite a number of famous bands through records, and I always imitated them. Once again, imitation. That was the -- that's why, to this day, I, I, I don't copy anybody, but I try to use my own, my own way of

playing, performing. And those years in Tucson was very instructive. I'm gettin' back to where I came from. I find myself temporarily where I came from, and in that way, I begin to be a little more aware of who I was, and my Indian-ness has never left me although I was away from the Indians in Chicago and I had forgotten my language.
